standard.title: Transfer skills to unfamiliar situations
standard.description: transfer and adapt skills and strategies from previous experiences to create successful outcomes in unfamiliar movement situations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can practise and apply leadership, collaboration and group decision-making in physical activities (AC9HP8M09). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to the metacognitive skill of deliberately transferring movement skills and strategies from known to unknown contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students transfer and adapt movement skills and strategies from previous experiences to create successful outcomes in unfamiliar movement situations.

nodes.label: Identifying transferable skills and strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify which skills and strategies from previous movement experiences are likely to transfer to an unfamiliar situation
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one skill or strategy from a familiar movement context and explain which elements are likely to transfer to a named unfamiliar situation
nodes.typical_width: Draw parallels between successful movement strategies in one sporting situation and how similar strategies could be used in a different sport; speculate on possible outcomes of innovative solutions based on past experience in outdoor or nature-based activities; identify which prior movement experiences are most relevant to a new challenge
wider: Systematically map transferable skills across two or more sport or movement contexts — identify what transfers directly, what needs adaptation, and what is genuinely new
Apply transfer thinking to an outdoor adventure activity (rope climbing, bushwalking, abseiling, kayaking) — identify which prior movement experiences are most relevant and why
Evaluate which aspects of a movement strategy are context-independent (transferable) versus context-specific (non-transferable) — build a framework for deciding what to transfer
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify what is transferable and why cannot deliberately apply transfer in Node 2 — they will act intuitively rather than strategically, and the evaluation of transfer success in Node 2 requires having predicted what would transfer first.

response_modes.reason: Transfer thinking requires explicit reasoning about what makes a skill or strategy portable — what are the underlying principles that apply across contexts, versus what is specific to the original context. Students who move to unfamiliar situations without this reasoning just try familiar things without knowing why. The structured reasoning investment is in building the transfer analysis: what is the skill, what principle underpins it, in what other contexts does that principle apply.

success_criteria: Names a specific skill or strategy from a familiar movement context
Identifies which elements transfer and explains the underlying principle that makes them transferable
Distinguishes between what transfers directly and what would need adaptation

nodes.label: Applying and evaluating transfer
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply transferred skills and strategies in unfamiliar situations and evaluate the success of the transfer
nodes.minimum_width: Apply at least one transferred skill or strategy in an unfamiliar movement situation; evaluate whether the transfer was successful and what adaptation was needed
nodes.typical_width: Attempt innovative solutions to movement challenges in unfamiliar situations based on past experience; reflect on the effectiveness of movement solutions and suggest improvements; propose how the solution can be transferred to other movement situations
wider: Apply transfer across multiple unfamiliar situations — compare which transfers worked better and build explanations for why some transfers succeed more readily than others
Evaluate a failed transfer attempt — identify what was assumed to transfer that didn't, and explain why; propose what would need to be different for the transfer to succeed
Lead a group through an unfamiliar movement challenge by deliberately applying and teaching transfer thinking — evaluate the group's success and your own leadership of the transfer process

response_modes.reason: Transfer capability builds through repeated practice of the transfer cycle across multiple unfamiliar situations. A single successful transfer does not develop the metacognitive skill — students need to experience both successful and unsuccessful transfers, and to reflect on what determined the outcome. The elaborations explicitly require reflection on effectiveness and proposals for further transfer.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-situation transfer comparison, failed transfer analysis, and leading group transfer thinking each add dimensions that single-transfer work does not. Students who engage the wider tier develop transfer as a deliberate metacognitive skill rather than an intuitive one — and develop the evaluative vocabulary to explain why some transfers work and others don't.
success_criteria: Attempts to apply a transferred skill or strategy in a named unfamiliar situation
Evaluates whether the transfer was successful — with specific reference to the outcome
Identifies what adaptation was needed and explains why the original form didn't transfer directly
